15: # Worked Decision-Tree Example
16: 
17: A compact, validator-safe decision-tree flowchart and a breakdown of why it satisfies the packet validator's label, connector, and width checks. This is overflow detail; `../../SKILL.md` is the authoritative workflow contract.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: This file gives one compact, validator-passing decision-tree flowchart, then breaks down why its labels, connectors, and box widths satisfy the packet validator's checks. Use it as a shape to model a real decision tree on — replace the support-triage content with sourced nodes rather than copying it verbatim.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. WORKED DECISION TREE
28: 
29: The example below borrows the decision-tree asset's shape: visible question nodes, explicit branch outcomes, retry or escalation handling, convergence, and terminal states. It uses `[YES]` and `[NO]` labels because the validator accepts those tokens or checkmarks for decision labels.
30: 
31: ```text
32: ╭────────────────────────────────────────────╮
33: │        SUPPORT REQUEST TRIAGE FLOW         │
34: ╰────────────────────────────────────────────╯
35: ↓
36: ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
37: │  Request Received                          │
38: │  • Ticket captured                         │
39: └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
40: ↓
41: ╱────────────╲
42: ╱ Decision:   ╲
43: ╱ Known Issue? ╲
44: ╲              ╱
45: ╲────────────╱
46: ├─ [YES] Known
47: │  ↓
48: │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
49: │  │  Send Known Resolution                     │
50: │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
51: │  ↓
52: │  ╭────────────────────────────────────────────╮
53: │  │  Ticket Closed                             │
54: │  ╰────────────────────────────────────────────╯
55: └─ [NO] Unknown
56:    ↓
57:    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
58:    │  Investigate                               │
59:    │  • Reproduce symptom                       │
60:    └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
61:    ↓
62:    ╱────────────╲
63:    ╱ Decision:   ╲
64:    ╱ Fix Found?   ╲
65:    ╲              ╱
66:    ╲────────────╱
67:    ├─ [YES] Fix
68:    │  ↓
69:    │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
70:    │  │  Send Resolution                           │
71:    │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
72:    │  ↓
73:    │  ╭────────────────────────────────────────────╮
74:    │  │  Ticket Closed                             │
75:    │  ╰────────────────────────────────────────────╯
76:    └─ [NO] Escalate
77:       ↓
78:       ╭────────────────────────────────────────────╮
79:       │  Escalated To Specialist                   │
80:       ╰────────────────────────────────────────────╯
81: ```
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## 3. WHY THIS EXAMPLE PASSES
86: 
87: The example is not a universal template. It is a compact model for validator-safe decisions; replace its support-triage content with real sourced nodes.
88: 
89: **Decision labels**:
90: - the question nodes include `Decision`, which triggers the validator's decision detection
91: - each outgoing branch includes `[YES]` or `[NO]`, which satisfies the accepted label forms
92: - descriptive words follow the required token, for example `[YES] Known`, so the branch is machine-checkable and readable
93: 
94: **Connectors**:
95: - `├─` and `└─` branch markers satisfy the validator's connector pattern
96: - `↓` arrows satisfy the validator's arrow pattern and keep the raw markdown readable
97: - terminal states are drawn instead of left implicit in prose
98: 
99: **Widths**:
100: - the title, action, and terminal boxes all share one width
101: - the decision diamonds reuse one smaller width
102: - with only two box widths in play, the diagram stays well below the width-variation warning threshold

15: # Theming a diagram from DESIGN.md
16: 
17: `DESIGN.md` is a style reference, not a diagram form. The diagram packet applies one locally
18: available v3 reference to a copy of a form: it never fetches a reference, never repaints the stock
19: forms, and never guesses a colour a reference did not hold.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: ### Purpose
26: 
27: Gives a diagram delivery the look of a measured or hand-written brand reference the same way a
28: chart delivery already gets it, with the diagram's own role vocabulary — structural chrome across
29: three skins — derived, gated and recorded rather than mapped across from the chart's series model.
30: 
31: ### When to Use
32: 
33: - A request names a `DESIGN.md`, a design system, or a look found somewhere that a reference
34:   generator has turned into a v3 reference file.
35: - A themed diagram copy is wanted for review while the stock corpus stays untouched.
36: - The stock look itself is wanted as one reference among several: `--default` is the reference the
37:   corpus's own palette is written down in.
38: 
39: ### Core Principle
40: 
41: A role is filled by what the reference says about it, and when the reference says nothing the role
42: is either derived mechanically from a role it did say something about, or it keeps the stock value
43: and the run says so by name. The stock accent's recorded departure is never re-derived into a pass
44: for a themed value.
45: 
46: ### Key Sources
47: 
48: - The applicator: [`apply-design-md.cjs`](../scripts/apply-design-md.cjs).
49: - The token source it reads on every run for roles, gates and departures:
50:   [`diagram-palette.json`](../assets/style-reference/harness-diagram/diagram-palette.json).
51: - Contrast arithmetic, shared with the corpus checker: [`color-gates.cjs`](../scripts/color-gates.cjs).
52: - The carried reference `--default` derives from and the corpus was written from:
53:   [`harness-diagram/DESIGN.md`](../assets/style-reference/harness-diagram/DESIGN.md), whose
54:   [`origin.md`](../assets/style-reference/harness-diagram/origin.md) records that it was authored
55:   from the packet's palette rather than measured from a product.
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 2. THE COMMAND
60: 
61: ```bash

102: | Reference section | Required shape | Used for |
103: | --- | --- | --- |
104: | `## Tokens — Colors` | `Name`, `Value`, `Token`, `Role` table | Tier-one role declarations, and the row pool every selection rule measures |
105: | `## Tokens — Typography` | First typeface heading plus its immediate `Substitute` line | Shape check only; a diagram carries its font stacks as CSS variables |
106: | `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes` → `### Border Radius` | `Element`, `Value` table | Shape check only; a diagram carries its corners as inline attributes |

109: reference with fewer than four usable six-digit colour rows is refused the same way. Six-digit
110: values are the rows the selection rules can measure; the alpha-composed `rule`, `rule-solid` and

124: shape `--color-<role>`, `--color-<role> (dark)` or `--color-<role> (terminal)`, fills that role
125: verbatim from the same row's `Value`. A bare `--color-<role>` fills the light skin; `(dark)` and
126: `(terminal)` fill the skin they name. A Token cell naming anything else — a generic
127: `--color-primary`, a chart token, a custom-property this vocabulary does not define — is ignored,
128: and the role falls through to tier two.

131: row, derive a value mechanically, or fall back. Tier two is unchanged by the tier-one rule, and it
132: is the whole derivation for a reference written in another vocabulary.

137: on their own, because they were written to generalise over a generic table and the corpus is one
138: particular reading of one particular table:

149: weakening the rules: a reference that says `--color-paper` has answered the question `paper` asks,
150: and the tier-two rules stay the answer for a reference that has not.

157: `isChromatic` (saturation ≥ 24%) and "lightest/darkest" are the same primitives the chart sibling

183: 
184: ## 6. THE TERMINAL CONDITIONAL
185: 
186: The terminal skin is a third, structurally different register with no chart equivalent, and it is
187: themed only when the reference actually supports a dark environment. Both conditions must hold:
188: 
189: 1. The reference declares dark support — a `**Theme:**` line naming dark, or a sibling `tokens.json`
190:    with a supported `darkMode`.
191: 2. The table supplies at least four distinct usable neutral or background-tagged rows darker than
192:    its chosen light `paper`.

194: When either fails, all nine terminal roles keep the token source's values and the run prints a
195: `NOTE` naming the reason. A terminal-skinned form named through `--forms` fails by name instead,
196: because a caller who asked for that form specifically asked for a skin no reference qualified; under
197: `--all` the form is written with its stock bytes and the note says so.
198:

200: prevent: a delivery that claims a dark register the reference never described.

202: ---

204: ## 7. GATES BEFORE WRITING
205: 
206: Thresholds are read from `diagram-palette.json` on every run; the colour arithmetic is the same
207: module the corpus checker uses, so one transfer curve and one rounding produce both results.
208: 
209: - `textOnPaper` (4.5:1) applies to `ink`, `muted` and `soft` — the roles that may carry text.
210: - `markOnPaper` (3.0:1) applies to `accent` and every other gated role against its own ground.
211: - `accentAgainstInk` (1.5:1) applies to `accent` against the skin's `ink`.
212: - The token source's `ungated` list, its structure roles (`paper`, `page`, a second paper tone,
213:   terminal `soft`) and its non-hex composed roles are not measured: `backend-fill`, `bar`,
214:   `border`, `high-level-chevron`, `page`, `rule`, `rule-solid` and `series-1..5` sit in that list.
215: - A value under its gate is excused only when the skin, the role and the measured ratio all match a
216:   recorded departure. Three are recorded: the light accent at 2.863:1, the light `soft` at 3.48:1
217:   and the terminal `soft` at 2.76:1. A themed value that lands on one of those measurements would be
218:   excused the same way; a themed accent that misses the mark gate is refused instead.
219: 
220: Every selected form's full palette is derived and gated in memory before any file is written. One
221: failure anywhere aborts the whole run:
222: 
223: ```text
224: FAILURE template light accent ratio=1.89:1 gate=markOnPaper 3:1 against #f5f5f5: nearest clearing value #ca7956
225: RESULT: FAILED
226: ```

228: A pass prints one `MAPPING` line per role per skin — which tier filled it, from which row, and its
229: ratio against the ground — then writes the selected forms and ends with `RESULT: PASSED`. Exit code
230: `0` is a pass, `1` is a failed gate, `2` is an unusable input (no reference, a URL, a missing
231: heading, a refusal to write into the stock directory).
232: 
233: ---
234: 
235: ## 8. WHAT CHANGES IN A DELIVERY
236: 
237: ### The block and the literals
238: 
239: The palette block's own declarations are rewritten value by value, preserving every other byte of
240: each line: indentation, role name, spacing before the value and any trailing comment.
241: 
242: Outside the block, every literal a role's stock value matches is remapped too, because the corpus
243: keeps some roles as plain hex in the markup — `#4f5d75` on an arrow marker, `#eb6c36` on an accent
244: marker, `#ffffff` on a panel — and a block-only substitution would leave those marks stock. The map
245: is built from the stock skin's values, so a themed literal is always recognised against the bytes
246: the file actually carries. A six-digit hex literal the stock skin does not carry is refused by name
247: rather than guessed; a shorthand or eight-digit hex is not a role literal and is left alone.
248: 
249: ### Provenance, and when it is written
250: 
251: A theme that repaints the block rewrites its marker and records where the values came from:
252: 
253: ```css
254: /* DIAGRAM_PALETTE:BEGIN skin=light system=design-md */
255: /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=.skilled/skills/.../DESIGN.md sha256=<64 hex> generator=1.0.0.0 */
256: ```
257: 
258: The path is repository-relative when the reference lives inside the repository, and the one given on
259: the command line otherwise. The hash is the SHA-256 of the input file.
260: 
261: A reference that derives exactly what the block already carries writes neither: the block keeps its
262: stock marker and no comment is inserted. Provenance says where a value came from, and a block whose
263: values are the file's own has nothing to vouch for. That is also what makes the identity run
264: observable — `--default` writes the stock bytes because the carried reference is the corpus's own
265: palette written down, not because a comparison was loosened. The rule is per block: a reference that
266: repaints one skin and not another stamps only the block it changed.
267: 
268: A form that already carries `system=<id>` is refused by name; theming is applied to a stock form.
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 9. RELATED

275:   it repaints the same corpus from `diagram-palette.json` and is unchanged by this path.
276: - [`check-diagram-corpus.cjs`](../scripts/check-diagram-corpus.cjs) — the corpus checker, including

279:   still speaks.
280: - [`foundations/derivation-record.md`](foundations/derivation-record.md) — why each stock value is
281:   what it is.

186: The terminal skin is a third, structurally different register with no chart equivalent, and it is
187: themed only when the reference actually supports a dark environment. Both conditions must hold:
188: 
189: 1. The reference declares dark support — a `**Theme:**` line naming dark, or a sibling `tokens.json`
190:    with a supported `darkMode`.
191: 2. The table supplies at least four distinct usable neutral or background-tagged rows darker than
192:    its chosen light `paper`.
193: 
194: When either fails, all nine terminal roles keep the token source's values and the run prints a
195: `NOTE` naming the reason. A terminal-skinned form named through `--forms` fails by name instead,
196: because a caller who asked for that form specifically asked for a skin no reference qualified; under
197: `--all` the form is written with its stock bytes and the note says so.
198: 
199: Four dark layers cannot be invented from a light-only table. That is the failure this gate exists to
200: prevent: a delivery that claims a dark register the reference never described.
201: 
202: ---
203: 
204: ## 7. GATES BEFORE WRITING
205: 
206: Thresholds are read from `diagram-palette.json` on every run; the colour arithmetic is the same
207: module the corpus checker uses, so one transfer curve and one rounding produce both results.
208: 
209: - `textOnPaper` (4.5:1) applies to `ink`, `muted` and `soft` — the roles that may carry text.
210: - `markOnPaper` (3.0:1) applies to `accent` and every other gated role against its own ground.
211: - `accentAgainstInk` (1.5:1) applies to `accent` against the skin's `ink`.
212: - The token source's `ungated` list, its structure roles (`paper`, `page`, a second paper tone,
213:   terminal `soft`) and its non-hex composed roles are not measured: `backend-fill`, `bar`,
214:   `border`, `high-level-chevron`, `page`, `rule`, `rule-solid` and `series-1..5` sit in that list.
215: - A value under its gate is excused only when the skin, the role and the measured ratio all match a
216:   recorded departure. Three are recorded: the light accent at 2.863:1, the light `soft` at 3.48:1
217:   and the terminal `soft` at 2.76:1. A themed value that lands on one of those measurements would be
218:   excused the same way; a themed accent that misses the mark gate is refused instead.
219: 
220: Every selected form's full palette is derived and gated in memory before any file is written. One
221: failure anywhere aborts the whole run:
222: 
223: ```text
224: FAILURE template light accent ratio=1.89:1 gate=markOnPaper 3:1 against #f5f5f5: nearest clearing value #ca7956
225: RESULT: FAILED
226: ```
227: 
228: A pass prints one `MAPPING` line per role per skin — which tier filled it, from which row, and its
229: ratio against the ground — then writes the selected forms and ends with `RESULT: PASSED`. Exit code
230: `0` is a pass, `1` is a failed gate, `2` is an unusable input (no reference, a URL, a missing
231: heading, a refusal to write into the stock directory).
232: 
233: ---
234: 
235: ## 8. WHAT CHANGES IN A DELIVERY
236: 
237: ### The block and the literals
238: 
239: The palette block's own declarations are rewritten value by value, preserving every other byte of
240: each line: indentation, role name, spacing before the value and any trailing comment.
241: 
242: Outside the block, every literal a role's stock value matches is remapped too, because the corpus
243: keeps some roles as plain hex in the markup — `#4f5d75` on an arrow marker, `#eb6c36` on an accent
244: marker, `#ffffff` on a panel — and a block-only substitution would leave those marks stock. The map
245: is built from the stock skin's values, so a themed literal is always recognised against the bytes
246: the file actually carries. A six-digit hex literal the stock skin does not carry is refused by name
247: rather than guessed; a shorthand or eight-digit hex is not a role literal and is left alone.
248: 
249: ### Provenance, and when it is written
250: 
251: A theme that repaints the block rewrites its marker and records where the values came from:
252: 
253: ```css
254: /* DIAGRAM_PALETTE:BEGIN skin=light system=design-md */
255: /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=.skilled/skills/.../DESIGN.md sha256=<64 hex> generator=1.0.0.0 */
256: ```
257: 
258: The path is repository-relative when the reference lives inside the repository, and the one given on
259: the command line otherwise. The hash is the SHA-256 of the input file.
260: 
261: A reference that derives exactly what the block already carries writes neither: the block keeps its
262: stock marker and no comment is inserted. Provenance says where a value came from, and a block whose
263: values are the file's own has nothing to vouch for. That is also what makes the identity run
264: observable — `--default` writes the stock bytes because the carried reference is the corpus's own
265: palette written down, not because a comparison was loosened. The rule is per block: a reference that
266: repaints one skin and not another stamps only the block it changed.
267: 
268: A form that already carries `system=<id>` is refused by name; theming is applied to a stock form.
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 9. RELATED
273: 
274: - [`apply-diagram-tokens.cjs`](../scripts/apply-diagram-tokens.cjs) — the stock-palette applicator;
275:   it repaints the same corpus from `diagram-palette.json` and is unchanged by this path.
276: - [`check-diagram-corpus.cjs`](../scripts/check-diagram-corpus.cjs) — the corpus checker, including
277:   the `derivation-gates` family that gates a palette block's inline values.

279:   still speaks.

13: # Diagram Palette Derivation Record
14: 
15: Where every diagram-skin color comes from, and what stays fixed when the skin changes.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: Every color role the diagram skin themes appears in exactly one of three lists: LIGHT (§2), DARK (§3) and TERMINAL (§4). Every value in those lists is exactly one of four kinds:
22: 
23: - **primary**: a value chosen by hand, stated verbatim. A re-theme replaces primaries and nothing else.
24: - **derived**: computed from a primary by a stated rule, for example `ink` at an alpha. This is stricter than the style guide's prose, which also calls `soft` and `link` "derived" although no rule reproduces them.
25: - **fixed**: a value that never re-themes. Onboarding and hand-edits of the skin leave it untouched.
26: - **untokenized** used to be a fourth kind, applying to files rather than values: it marked a file exempt from this record because it carried its own fixed skin. The key is gone. The one file that held the exemption carried a tone the dark skin never defined, at 4.44:1 under the text gate, so the exemption was hiding a defect rather than recording a decision; repointing that tone onto the dark muted role emptied the list and the key went with it. Every form now regenerates from this record.
27: 
28: The opt-in series palette for multi-series charts lives in the style guide, not here. The applicator of a later phase reads this record, and the corpus checker re-derives every value marked **derived** from the primaries recorded here.
29: 
30: ---
31: 
32: ## 2. LIGHT
33: 
34: | Role | Value | Kind | Rule or source |
35: |---|---|---|---|
36: | `paper` | `#f5f5f5` | primary | White-smoke from the five-color brand palette |
37: | `paper-2` | `#ececec` | primary | Hand-picked, one step darker than `paper` |
38: | `ink` | `#2d3142` | primary | Jet-black from the brand palette |
39: | `muted` | `#4f5d75` | primary | Blue-slate from the brand palette |
40: | `soft` | `#7a8399` | primary | Hand-picked, a lighter slate in the blue-slate family |
41: | `rule` | `rgba(45,49,66,0.12)` | derived | `ink` at 0.12 |
42: | `rule-solid` | `rgba(79,93,117,0.25)` | derived | `muted` at 0.25; the templates' value, which settles the disagreement |
43: | `accent` | `#eb6c36` | primary | Atomic-tangerine from the brand palette |
44: | `accent-tint` | `rgba(235,108,54,0.08)` | derived | `accent` at 0.08 |
45: | `link` | `#2e5aa8` | primary | Hand-picked, a saturated variant in the blue-slate hue family |
46: | `backend-fill` | `#ffffff` | primary | The backend/API/step node fill; 40 occurrences in 13 files; never a paper substitute |
47: | `high-level-chevron` | `#3d4460` | primary | Type-scoped to `type-high-level` only |
48: 
49: ---
50: 
51: ## 3. DARK
52: 
53: | Role | Value | Kind | Rule or source |
54: |---|---|---|---|
55: | `paper` | `#2d3142` | primary | Jet-black from the brand palette, the light `ink` value reused |
56: | `ink` | `#f5f5f5` | primary | White-smoke from the brand palette, the light `paper` value reused |
57: | `muted` | `#bfc0c0` | primary | Silver from the brand palette |
58: | `accent` | `#f08a59` | primary | Hand-picked; not a lightness shift of the light accent |
59: | `link` | `#6a95d8` | primary | Hand-picked, a brighter counterpart of the light `link` |
60: 
61: Five primaries, and no derived roles. The dark drawing does use translucent forms of these — eleven
62: distinct alphas of ink, muted and accent across the one dark form — but they are not roles and do not
63: need to be. Both applicators match a translucent value by its channels and re-emit it at whatever
64: alpha the drawing chose, so a repaint carries every one of them without any of them being named.
65: 
66: This section used to list `paper-2`, `soft`, `rule`, `rule-solid` and `accent-tint` as dark roles.
67: Two of them named values no form has ever drawn; the other three named three alphas out of eleven,
68: which made the choice of those three arbitrary. A record that declares roles the token source does
69: not define is a record a themed block cannot satisfy: declaring the documented `--color-paper-2` in a
70: dark block is refused by the corpus check, because the skin has no such role.
71: 
72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ## 4. TERMINAL
76: 
77: The terminal skin is a second, fixed skin. You opt into it per diagram, and onboarding never touches it.
78: 
79: | Role | Value | Kind | Rule or source |
80: |---|---|---|---|
81: | `terminal-page` | `#0a0a0a` | fixed | Page background behind the window |
82: | `terminal-paper` | `#141414` | fixed | Window body, node fill |
83: | `terminal-bar` | `#1b1b1b` | fixed | Titlebar strip |
84: | `terminal-border` | `#2b2b2b` | fixed | Window border, hairlines |
85: | `terminal-ink` | `#f5f5f5` | fixed | Primary text, primary stroke, same white-smoke as the default light `ink` |
86: | `terminal-muted` | `#9a9a9a` | fixed | Secondary text, sublabels, ring stroke |
87: | `terminal-soft` | `#5c5c5c` | fixed | Tertiary: inactive dots, spokes |
88: | `terminal-accent` | `#ff5a36` | fixed | The one accent: focal station, prompt sign, active dot |
89: | `terminal-accent-tint` | `rgba(255,90,54,0.12)` | derived | `terminal-accent` at 0.12, the fill for accent-bordered boxes |
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 5. GATES
94: 
95: | Gate | Threshold | Applies to |
96: |---|---|---|
97: | `text-on-paper` | 4.5:1 | `ink`, `muted`, and any text role against its ground |
98: | `mark-on-paper` | 3.0:1 | Any stroke or fill that carries meaning |
99: | `accent-against-ink` | 1.5:1 | The `accent` wherever it meets an `ink`-weight ground |
100: | `text-on-mark` | 4.5:1 | A label set on a coloured mark rather than on the paper: a typed chip, a filled badge |
101: | hairlines | ungated | `rule` and `rule-solid`, decoration reviewed by eye |
102: 
103: `text-on-mark` was added after a reader measured white chip labels against the text gate by analogy
104: and found one under it. The analogy was sound and the gate was missing, which is the worse of the two
105: problems: a rule applied by eye is a rule that holds only while someone is looking. Series values
106: stay ungated against the paper, because a series mark carries no text; a series value used as a chip
107: fill is a different use and clears this gate or it does not ship. The one that did not, the second
108: series, moved two points darker — invisible at a glance, 4.44:1 to 4.56:1 against white, and better
109: against the paper as well.
110: 
111: ### Recorded departures
112: 
113: | Departure | Measures | Note |
114: |---|---|---|
115: | `accent` (#eb6c36) on `paper` (#f5f5f5) | 2.863:1 | Against the 3.0:1 mark gate; kept as the brand accent by decision; never re-derived |
116: | `soft` (#7a8399) on `paper` | 3.48:1 | Above the 3.0:1 mark gate, below the 4.5:1 text gate. May not carry sublabel or eyebrow text. |
117: | `terminal-soft` (#5c5c5c) on `terminal-paper` (#141414) | 2.76:1 | Decoration: inactive dots and spokes. Never carries text, so the text gate does not apply; recorded rather than exempted so the number is on the page. |
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 6. WHAT HOLDS THE STARTERS TO THIS RECORD
122: 
123: This section used to pin each starter file by sha256, on the theory that a pin which stops matching
124: means a starter changed without the record being updated. Nothing read the pins, and every one of
125: them was stale: fixing a defect in a starter changes its bytes, which is the point of fixing it.
126: 
127: What holds the relationship now is stronger and needs no upkeep. The applicator regenerates every
128: form from the values in this record, and the corpus check requires the result to equal the shipped
129: bytes exactly. A value that drifts from the record fails that comparison by name. A geometry change,
130: which a hash would have flagged and a reader would then have waved through, is not a drift at all.
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ## 7. TOLERANCES
135: 
136: Derived alphas are exact: a value recorded as `ink` at 0.12 must re-derive to `rgba(45,49,66,0.12)` with no rounding and no alternate notation. Contrast ratios are compared at two decimals, so 2.863:1 is recorded in full but gates as 2.86 against 3.0.

99: | `accent-against-ink` | 1.5:1 | The `accent` wherever it meets an `ink`-weight ground |
100: | `text-on-mark` | 4.5:1 | A label set on a coloured mark rather than on the paper: a typed chip, a filled badge |
101: | hairlines | ungated | `rule` and `rule-solid`, decoration reviewed by eye |
102: 
103: `text-on-mark` was added after a reader measured white chip labels against the text gate by analogy
104: and found one under it. The analogy was sound and the gate was missing, which is the worse of the two
105: problems: a rule applied by eye is a rule that holds only while someone is looking. Series values
106: stay ungated against the paper, because a series mark carries no text; a series value used as a chip
107: fill is a different use and clears this gate or it does not ship. The one that did not, the second
108: series, moved two points darker — invisible at a glance, 4.44:1 to 4.56:1 against white, and better
109: against the paper as well.
110: 
111: ### Recorded departures
112: 
113: | Departure | Measures | Note |
114: |---|---|---|
115: | `accent` (#eb6c36) on `paper` (#f5f5f5) | 2.863:1 | Against the 3.0:1 mark gate; kept as the brand accent by decision; never re-derived |
116: | `soft` (#7a8399) on `paper` | 3.48:1 | Above the 3.0:1 mark gate, below the 4.5:1 text gate. May not carry sublabel or eyebrow text. |
117: | `terminal-soft` (#5c5c5c) on `terminal-paper` (#141414) | 2.76:1 | Decoration: inactive dots and spokes. Never carries text, so the text gate does not apply; recorded rather than exempted so the number is on the page. |
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 6. WHAT HOLDS THE STARTERS TO THIS RECORD
122: 
123: This section used to pin each starter file by sha256, on the theory that a pin which stops matching
124: means a starter changed without the record being updated. Nothing read the pins, and every one of
125: them was stale: fixing a defect in a starter changes its bytes, which is the point of fixing it.
126: 
127: What holds the relationship now is stronger and needs no upkeep. The applicator regenerates every
128: form from the values in this record, and the corpus check requires the result to equal the shipped
129: bytes exactly. A value that drifts from the record fails that comparison by name. A geometry change,
130: which a hash would have flagged and a reader would then have waved through, is not a drift at all.
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ## 7. TOLERANCES
135: 
136: Derived alphas are exact: a value recorded as `ink` at 0.12 must re-derive to `rgba(45,49,66,0.12)` with no rounding and no alternate notation. Contrast ratios are compared at two decimals, so 2.863:1 is recorded in full but gates as 2.86 against 3.0.

57: 
58: > *"Onboard the diagram skill to my site — `https://example.com`"*

63: 
64: ### Step 2 — extract colors and fonts
65: 
66: ### Colors
67: 
68: Parse the rendered CSS and screenshot:
69: 
70: - **Background color** of `<body>` or the dominant large region → `paper`
71: - **Primary text color** (body text) → `ink`
72: - **Secondary text color** (captions, meta) → `muted`
73: - **Most-used brand color** (CTA button, link, heading accent) → `accent`
74: - **Container / card background** slightly darker than paper → `paper-2`
75: - **Border / hairline color** → `rule` (convert to rgba of ink at ~0.12 opacity)
76: 
77: Prefer CSS custom properties when the site exposes them (`:root { --accent: …; }`). Otherwise pull via rendered `getComputedStyle` samples or a color-histogram pass over the screenshot.
78: 
79: ### Fonts
80: 
81: Read the rendered `font-family` stack of:
82: 
83: - `<h1>` → `title` family
84: - `<body>` → `node-name` family
85: - `<code>`, `<pre>`, or any mono-styled element → `sublabel` family

94: |---|---|---|
95: | paper | `#f8f6f0` | high |
96: | ink | `#111111` | high |
97: | muted | `#6b6b68` | medium |
98: | accent | `#c73a2b` | high |
99: | … | … | … |
100: 
101: Flag low-confidence guesses so the user can correct before applying.
102: 
103: ### Constraint checks
104: 
105: Before writing, validate:
106: 
107: - **AA contrast**: `ink` on `paper` ≥ 4.5:1. `muted` on `paper` ≥ 4.5:1 for body text.

109: - **paper ≠ pure white**: if the site uses `#ffffff`, fall back to `#fafaf7` to preserve Schematic's warm-neutral feel — or ask the user to confirm pure-white is intentional.

122: +| `ink`    | `#111111` | `#efeee7` |
123: +| `accent` | `#c73a2b` | `#e05440` |
124: ```

127: 
128: ### Step 5 — apply
129: 
130: Write the new tokens to `style-guide.md`. Suggest running the `/regenerate-examples` flow (if it exists) or rebuilding one example to verify the new skin reads cleanly.

134: 1. Open the gallery and confirm the new palette feels coherent across all 27 types.

146: ## 3. SKILL SOURCE
147: 
148: Extract tokens from an installed Agent Skill that carries its own design system (e.g. a `brand-design` or `ui-kit` skill).
149: 
150: ### Invocation
151: 
152: > *"Onboard the diagram skill from my `acme-design` skill"*
153: 
154: Or the gate offers this as option (b) and the user names the skill.

156: ### Step 1 — locate the skill
157: 
158: Use the installed-skill location exposed by the current agent when available. Otherwise search locations for the active harness:
159: 
160: **Pi:**
161: 
162: 1. `~/.pi/agent/skills/<skill-name>/` and `~/.agents/skills/<skill-name>/` (user installs)
163: 2. `.pi/skills/<skill-name>/` in the current directory, plus `.agents/skills/<skill-name>/` from the current directory through the repo root (project installs)
164: 3. Package paths listed in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` or `.pi/settings.json`; managed packages live under `~/.pi/agent/git/`, `~/.pi/agent/npm/`, `.pi/git/`, or `.pi/npm/`
165: 
166: **Claude Code:**
167: 
168: 1. `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/` (user install)
169: 2. `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/` (project install)
170: 
171: **OpenCode:**
172: 
173: 1. `~/.config/opencode/skills/<skill-name>/` (user install)
174: 2. `.skilled/skills/<skill-name>/` (project install)
175: 
176: Finally, check any path the user provides explicitly. If the skill is still not found, ask the user to confirm the name or provide its path.
177: 
178: ### Step 2 — read token sources
179: 
180: Glob the skill directory for any of these files and read them all:
181: 
182: | Priority | Pattern | What to look for |
183: |---|---|---|
184: | 1 | `*.css`, `colors*.css`, `tokens.css` | CSS custom properties in `:root { --color-*: …; }` |
185: | 2 | `tokens.json`, `design-tokens.json`, `*.tokens.json` | Style Dictionary / Figma token JSON |
186: | 3 | `SKILL.md`, `README.md` | Markdown tables listing colors, fonts, hex values |
187: | 4 | `style-guide.md`, `*design*.md` | Any narrative design documentation |
188: | 5 | `*.html` (preview/example files) | Inline `<style>` blocks — scan `:root` and `body` rules |
189: 
190: Read all matches and merge — CSS custom properties take priority over inferred values from HTML.
191: 
192: ### Step 3 — extract colors and fonts
193: 
194: **From CSS custom properties:**
195: Map variable names to semantic roles using name-heuristics:
196: 
197: | If the variable name contains… | Map to role |
198: |---|---|
199: | `background`, `bg`, `paper`, `surface`, `canvas` | `paper` |
200: | `foreground`, `text`, `body`, `ink`, `on-surface` | `ink` |
201: | `muted`, `subtle`, `secondary`, `caption` | `muted` |
202: | `accent`, `brand`, `primary`, `cta`, `highlight` | `accent` |
203: | `border`, `rule`, `divider`, `outline` | `rule` |
204: | `mono`, `code`, `pre` | `sublabel` font |
205: 
206: **From JSON tokens:** follow the same heuristics on key names. If the JSON follows Style Dictionary format (`{ "color": { "brand": { "value": "#…" } } }`), flatten the path and apply heuristics to the leaf key.
207: 
208: **From Markdown tables:** look for rows with hex values (`#rrggbb`) adjacent to role-like words. A row like `| accent | #eb6c36 |` maps directly.
209: 
210: **Fonts:** look for `font-family` rules, `@import` or `@font-face` declarations, and Markdown mentions of font names alongside size/weight.
211: 
212: ### Step 4 — map, validate, propose diff
213: 
214: Same as the URL method: fill the role table, run contrast checks, show the diff, ask for approval before writing.
215: 
216: ### When skill extraction is ambiguous
217: 
218: - **Skill has no CSS or token files**: fall back to reading all `.md` files and look for hex values mentioned in prose. Surface what you found and ask the user to confirm mappings before applying.
219: - **Multiple accent candidates**: list them and ask the user to pick one. Don't guess.
220: - **Skill is dark-mode first**: ask whether to treat the dark values as the `paper`/`ink` defaults or to invert.
221: 
222: ---
223: 
224: ## 4. FOLDER SOURCE
225: 
226: Extract tokens from a local directory — a checked-out design system repo, a Figma export, or any folder the user points you at.
227: 
228: ### Invocation
229: 
230: > *"Onboard the diagram skill from my design system at `~/projects/brand/design-tokens/`"*
231: 
232: Or the gate offers this as option (c) and the user provides the path.
233: 
234: ### Step 1 — discover files
235: 
236: Glob the folder (recursively, up to 3 levels deep) for:
237: 
238: ```
239: **/*.css
240: **/*.scss        (read @forward / $variable declarations)
241: **/tokens.json
242: **/*.tokens.json
243: **/design-tokens.json
244: **/colors.json
245: **/*style-guide*.md
246: **/*design-system*.md
247: **/README.md
248: **/*.html        (scan <style> blocks only)
249: ```
250: 
251: If the result set is large (>20 files), prefer files in the root and files whose names contain `color`, `token`, `brand`, `palette`, `style`, or `theme`.
252: 
253: ### Step 2 — read and merge
254: 
255: Read every discovered file. Apply the same extraction logic as the Skill method (§3 → Step 3). CSS custom properties and JSON tokens take priority over inferred values from prose.
256: 
257: **SCSS variables:** treat `$variable-name: value;` the same as a CSS custom property — apply name heuristics to `$variable-name`.
258: 
259: **Figma token JSON** (Figma Tokens Plugin format):
260: 
261: ```json
262: { "colors": { "brand": { "primary": { "value": "#eb6c36", "type": "color" } } } }
263: ```
264: 
265: Walk the tree; the leaf `value` fields are the colors, the path segments supply the role heuristic.
266: 
267: ### Step 3 — map, validate, propose diff
268: 
269: Same as the URL method: run contrast checks, show the full diff against current `style-guide.md`, and write only after the user approves.
270: 
271: ### When folder extraction is ambiguous
272: 
273: - **No structured token files, only prose docs**: read every `.md` in the root and extract hex values found near role-like words. Show the user a table of what you inferred — don't silently apply uncertain mappings.
274: - **Multiple themes / color schemes found**: list them, ask the user which one to use as the diagram skin.
275: - **Folder has zero readable files**: tell the user and ask for a more specific path or switch to manual token entry.
276: 
277: ---
278: 
279: ## 5. FUTURE: PER-PROJECT SKINS
280: 
281: If the user wants multiple skins (one per project), duplicate `style-guide.md` as `style-guides/<project>.md` and add a header comment pointing the build to the active one. That's a v5.2 feature — for now, one skin per skill install.

199: | `background`, `bg`, `paper`, `surface`, `canvas` | `paper` |
200: | `foreground`, `text`, `body`, `ink`, `on-surface` | `ink` |
201: | `muted`, `subtle`, `secondary`, `caption` | `muted` |
202: | `accent`, `brand`, `primary`, `cta`, `highlight` | `accent` |
203: | `border`, `rule`, `divider`, `outline` | `rule` |
204: | `mono`, `code`, `pre` | `sublabel` font |
205: 
206: **From JSON tokens:** follow the same heuristics on key names. If the JSON follows Style Dictionary format (`{ "color": { "brand": { "value": "#…" } } }`), flatten the path and apply heuristics to the leaf key.
207: 
208: **From Markdown tables:** look for rows with hex values (`#rrggbb`) adjacent to role-like words. A row like `| accent | #eb6c36 |` maps directly.
209: 
210: **Fonts:** look for `font-family` rules, `@import` or `@font-face` declarations, and Markdown mentions of font names alongside size/weight.
211:

213: 
214: Same as the URL method: fill the role table, run contrast checks, show the diff, ask for approval before writing.
215:

217: 
218: - **Skill has no CSS or token files**: fall back to reading all `.md` files and look for hex values mentioned in prose. Surface what you found and ask the user to confirm mappings before applying.

221: 
222: ---
223: 
224: ## 4. FOLDER SOURCE
225: 
226: Extract tokens from a local directory — a checked-out design system repo, a Figma export, or any folder the user points you at.
227: 
228: ### Invocation
229: 
230: > *"Onboard the diagram skill from my design system at `~/projects/brand/design-tokens/`"*
231: 
232: Or the gate offers this as option (c) and the user provides the path.
233: 
234: ### Step 1 — discover files
235: 
236: Glob the folder (recursively, up to 3 levels deep) for:
237: 
238: ```
239: **/*.css
240: **/*.scss        (read @forward / $variable declarations)
241: **/tokens.json
242: **/*.tokens.json
243: **/design-tokens.json
244: **/colors.json
245: **/*style-guide*.md
246: **/*design-system*.md

272: 
273: - **No structured token files, only prose docs**: read every `.md` in the root and extract hex values found near role-like words. Show the user a table of what you inferred — don't silently apply uncertain mappings.

276: 
277: ---
278: 
279: ## 5. FUTURE: PER-PROJECT SKINS
280: 
281: If the user wants multiple skins (one per project), duplicate `style-guide.md` as `style-guides/<project>.md` and add a header comment pointing the build to the active one. That's a v5.2 feature — for now, one skin per skill install.

17: # Output Spec — format × size × detail × audience
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: Four dials decide what an imported diagram becomes. Set them **before** redrawing — they change the deliverable, layout, type ramp, node count, and wording.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 2. FORMAT
26: 
27: | Format | Deliverable | Keeps | Drops |
28: |---|---|---|---|
29: | `html` | self-contained `.html` (default) | header, diagram, summary cards, footer, live fonts | nothing |
30: | `svg` | `.svg` next to the source | the `<svg>` node, vector text | editorial wrapper; fonts substitute in offline tools |
31: | `png` | `.png` at `device_scale_factor` | pixels exactly as the browser renders them | vector editability |
32: | `html+png` | both | — | — |
33: 
34: Always generate the HTML first — `svg` and `png` are produced *from* it via [`export.md`](../import-export/export.md). Never hand-author an SVG file directly; the HTML is the source of truth and the only artifact the taste gate (SKILL.md SUCCESS CRITERIA) is written against.
35: 
36: Pick by destination:
37: 
38: | Destination | Format | Size preset |
39: |---|---|---|
40: | Blog post, README, docs site | `html` (embed) or `png` | `doc-inline` |
41: | Keynote / PowerPoint / Google Slides | `png` @2 | `slide-16x9` |
42: | Figma / Illustrator / further editing | `svg` | `fit` |
43: | X / LinkedIn / OG link card | `png` @2 | `social-og` |
44: | Printed handout, PDF deck | `png` @3 | `print-a4-landscape` |
45: | Confluence / Notion / internal wiki | `png` @2 | `doc-wide` |
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## 3. SIZE
50: 
51: The preset sets the SVG `viewBox`. Every value below is divisible by 4, so the 4px grid rule in SKILL.md HOW IT WORKS still holds.
52: 
53: | Preset | viewBox | Aspect | PNG @2 | Type ramp | Use |
54: |---|---|---|---|---|---|
55: | `doc-inline` (default) | `0 0 960 600` | 8:5 | 1920×1200 | standard | Body-width diagram in a post or README |
56: | `doc-wide` | `0 0 1280 720` | 16:9 | 2560×1440 | standard | Full-width docs, wiki pages |
57: | `slide-16x9` | `0 0 1280 720` | 16:9 | 2560×1440 | presentation | Deck slide, projected |
58: | `slide-4x3` | `0 0 1024 768` | 4:3 | 2048×1536 | presentation | Legacy deck templates |
59: | `social-og` | `0 0 1200 632` | ~1.9:1 | 2400×1264 | presentation | Link preview card |
60: | `social-square` | `0 0 1080 1080` | 1:1 | 2160×2160 | presentation | Feed post, carousel |
61: | `print-a4-landscape` | `0 0 1120 792` | ~1.41:1 | @3 → 3360×2376 | print | A4 landscape, ~10mm margins at 96dpi |
62: | `print-letter-landscape` | `0 0 1056 816` | ~1.29:1 | @3 → 3168×2448 | print | US Letter landscape |
63: | `fit` | derived from content | any | @2 | standard | Vector hand-off; no fixed frame |
64: 
65: ### Deriving `fit`
66: 
67: Round the content bounding box **up** to the next multiple of 4, then add the fixed chrome: 40px outer margin on every side, plus 60px at the bottom for the legend strip. Never let the content touch the viewBox edge.
68: 
69: ### Type ramp per size class
70: 
71: Node names shrink relative to the canvas as it grows — resist that. Scale the ramp with the preset so a projected slide stays readable from the back row.
72: 
73: | Role | standard | presentation | print |
74: |---|---|---|---|
75: | Title (Instrument Serif) | 28 | 40 | 32 |
76: | Node name (Geist 600) | 12 | 16 | 12 |
77: | Sublabel (Geist Mono) | 9 | 12 | 9 |
78: | Arrow label (Geist Mono) | 8 | 12 | 8 |
79: | Eyebrow / tag (Geist Mono) | 8 | 8 | 8 |
80: | Node box min height | 48 | 64 | 48 |
81: | Min gap between nodes | 24 | 40 | 24 |
82: 
83: Presentation ramp implies fewer nodes — 16px names in 64px boxes eat the canvas. If a `slide-16x9` layout won't fit, that's the size dial telling you the detail dial is set too high; drop a level rather than shrinking the type.
84: 
85: ### Safe areas
86: 
87: - **All presets:** 40px outer margin; legend strip is the bottom 60px and nothing else lives there.
88: - **`social-og`:** keep the outer 64px clear on every side — link-card crops are unpredictable across platforms.
89: - **`slide-*`:** keep the bottom 80px clear if the deck template has a footer bar; ask if unsure.
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 4. DETAIL LEVEL
94: 
95: How much of the source survives. This is a *count* dial — it governs how many elements make it through, not how they're worded (that's §5).
96: 
97: | Level | Nodes | Edges | Sublabels | What survives |
98: |---|---|---|---|---|
99: | `faithful` (詳細) | ≤24, zoned | ≤32 | every port, protocol, version | Every distinct component in the source. Only exact duplicates merge. |
100: | `balanced` (default) | ≤12 | ≤16 | technical sublabel on ≤4 nodes | Components that carry the story; leaf clusters collapse to one node each. |
101: | `simplified` (簡略) | ≤7 | ≤9 | none | Capabilities and their sequence. Infrastructure disappears. |
102: 
103: `balanced` and `simplified` sit inside the standard complexity budget (SKILL.md HOW IT WORKS). **`faithful` deliberately exceeds it** — that's the trade, and it comes with conditions:
104: 
105: 1. **Zoning is mandatory.** Above 9 nodes, every node belongs to a labeled zone (2–4 zones, hairline-bordered, `paper-2` fill, mono uppercase zone label at top-left). An unzoned 20-node diagram is a wiring diagram, not a schematic.
106: 2. **Connector rules don't relax.** SKILL.md RULES connector rules still apply at 24 nodes. If you can't route it without overlaps, you're over the real ceiling — split.
107: 3. **Above 24 nodes, split.** Produce an overview (zones as nodes, `balanced` grammar) plus one detail diagram per zone. Name them `<base>-overview.html`, `<base>-<zone>.html`. Never ship a 40-node single canvas.
108: 4. **Accent stays at 2.** More nodes never buys more focal elements.
109: 
110: ### Degrade ladder
111: 
112: When the source has more than the level allows, cut in this order and stop as soon as you're under budget. Never cut ad hoc.
113: 
114: 1. **Decorative cells** — sticky notes, free-floating text, title blocks, watermarks, the source's own legend. (Notes worth keeping become annotation callouts — max 2, see [primitive-annotation.md](../primitives/primitive-annotation.md).)
115: 2. **Exact duplicates** — N identical workers/replicas/shards become one node labeled `Worker ×N`.
116: 3. **Leaf clusters** — a container whose children are all leaves collapses to the container: `Core Services` replaces its three boxes. The extractor lists these under *collapsible groups*.
117: 4. **Degree-1 sinks that don't change the story** — a monitoring hook, a log bucket, an archive tier.
118: 5. **Cross-cutting infrastructure** — logging, metrics, secrets, CI. At `simplified` these go without asking; at `balanced` keep at most one, and only if the diagram is about it.
119: 6. **Still over?** Split into overview + detail. Splitting beats shrinking.
120: 
121: Anything cut in steps 2–6 goes in the fidelity ledger (§6). Step 1 doesn't need reporting.
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 5. AUDIENCE LEVEL
126: 
127: Independent of the detail dial: the same 12 nodes get named differently for a platform team than for a steering committee. Detail sets *how many*; audience sets *what they're called*.
128: 
129: | Audience | Node names | Sublabels | Edge labels | Never |
130: |---|---|---|---|---|
131: | `engineer` | exact service / component names | protocol, port, version, image tag | `POST /v2/orders`, `SQL`, `gRPC` | Vague verbs like "connects to" |
132: | `mixed` (default) | component names, expanded acronyms | technology only where it changes a decision | plain verbs — `verifies`, `writes`, `notifies` | Ports, versions, internal codenames |
133: | `executive` | capabilities and outcomes | none | business verbs — `approves`, `pays out` | Vendor names, infrastructure, protocols |
134: 
135: Worked example — the same node through all three:
136: 
137: | Audience | Node name | Sublabel |
138: |---|---|---|
139: | `engineer` | `Auth Service` | `JWT · RS256 · :8443` |
140: | `mixed` | `Auth Service` | `token check` |
141: | `executive` | `Sign-in` | — |
142: 
143: Two rules that hold at every audience level:
144: 
145: - **Never invent detail to fill a slot.** If the source says `svc-04`, `executive` output says what it does only if you can tell from context — otherwise ask, don't guess a business name.
146: - **Keep the source's vocabulary for proper nouns.** Renaming `Kafka` to `Message Bus` is fine at `executive`; renaming it to `Event Grid` (a different product) is a factual error.
147: 
148: ### Non-Latin labels
149: 
150: Geist has no CJK coverage. When labels contain Japanese, Chinese, or Korean text, extend the family on those `<text>` elements — don't swap the whole skin:
151: 
152: ```svg
153: <text font-family="'Geist', 'Hiragino Sans', 'Noto Sans JP', 'Yu Gothic', sans-serif">認証サービス</text>
154: ```
155: 
156: For mono sublabels use `'Geist Mono', 'Noto Sans Mono CJK JP', monospace`. CJK glyphs render ~10% wider than Latin at the same size — budget box width accordingly, and prefer 12px names over 8px sublabels for CJK, which goes muddy below 10px.
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 6. FIDELITY LEDGER
161: 
162: Any time output is smaller than input — every `balanced` and `simplified` run, and most `faithful` ones — report what you cut, in chat, after the file path. Short and specific:
163: 
164: ```
165: Detail: balanced · 18 source nodes → 9 drawn
166: Merged:  worker-01..06 → "Ingest Worker ×6"
167: Collapsed: "Observability" group (Grafana, Loki, Tempo) → one node
168: Dropped: 2 sticky notes, CI pipeline (cross-cutting)
169: Kept in full: the request path (Client → Gateway → Orders → Postgres)
170: ```
171: 
172: The reader of the diagram can't see what's missing. The person who asked for it needs to.
173: 
174: ---
175: 
176: ## 7. CHECKLIST
177: 
178: Run alongside the SKILL.md SUCCESS CRITERIA taste gate.
179: 
180: - [ ] All four dials set — explicitly requested, inferred from the destination, or defaulted and stated?
181: - [ ] `viewBox` matches the size preset exactly, values divisible by 4?
182: - [ ] Type ramp matches the size class — not the standard ramp on a slide?
183: - [ ] 40px outer margin honoured (64px for `social-og`)?
184: - [ ] Node count inside the detail level's ceiling?
185: - [ ] `faithful` above 9 nodes → zoned, and split above 24?
186: - [ ] Node names, sublabels, and edge labels all at the same audience level?
187: - [ ] CJK labels given a font fallback?
188: - [ ] Fidelity ledger reported for anything cut?
189: - [ ] Diagram `<svg>` has `role="img"`, resolving `aria-labelledby`, a non-empty first-child `<title>`, a non-empty `<desc>`, and per-diagram/variant prefixed IDs?
190: - [ ] Requested non-HTML formats produced via [`export.md`](../import-export/export.md), not hand-authored?

148: ### Non-Latin labels
149: 
150: Geist has no CJK coverage. When labels contain Japanese, Chinese, or Korean text, extend the family on those `<text>` elements — don't swap the whole skin:
151: 
152: ```svg

154: ```
155: 
156: For mono sublabels use `'Geist Mono', 'Noto Sans Mono CJK JP', monospace`. CJK glyphs render ~10% wider than Latin at the same size — budget box width accordingly, and prefer 12px names over 8px sublabels for CJK, which goes muddy below 10px.

161: 
162: Any time output is smaller than input — every `balanced` and `simplified` run, and most `faithful` ones — report what you cut, in chat, after the file path. Short and specific:

166: Merged:  worker-01..06 → "Ingest Worker ×6"
167: Collapsed: "Observability" group (Grafana, Loki, Tempo) → one node
168: Dropped: 2 sticky notes, CI pipeline (cross-cutting)
169: Kept in full: the request path (Client → Gateway → Orders → Postgres)
170: ```

172: The reader of the diagram can't see what's missing. The person who asked for it needs to.
173: 
174: ---

22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`

26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95:

97: 
98: ```markdown

100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?

207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale

210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216:

218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```

230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882:

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:

999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073:

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199:
